claim: The Malay Basin is a Cenozoic rift basin located in the southern part of the South China Sea, formed during late Eocene/Oligocene extension.
source: Madon et al., 1999

claim: Group D, E, and F reservoirs are primarily fluvial-deltaic sandstones with high porosity (15-25%) and permeability.
source: NOC Carigali regional studies

claim: Fault seal risk is high for Group I reservoirs due to shale gouge ratio (SGR) variability under high fault displacement.
source: GEOX fault seal analysis, 2026

claim: A Class III AVO anomaly in the deep syn-rift Group M sandstones represents a high-saturation gas reservoir.
source: Seismic vision candidate ensemble

claim: Malay Basin is offshore east of Peninsular Malaysia and contributes about 40% of Malaysia’s hydrocarbon resources in the review period.
source: Madon, 2021

claim: Exploration history shows mature-basin creaming behavior: early giant discoveries, later smaller incremental additions.
source: Madon, 2021

claim: Malay Basin initiated by Late Eocene–Early Oligocene extension, high post-rift subsidence, >14 km sediment in deepest centre, E-W half-grabens influenced by Pre-Tertiary faults.
source: Madon, 2021

claim: Stratigraphy uses groups A–P; drilling reaches at least Group M; fill transitions from lacustrine/non-marine to coastal plain and shallow marine; K shale marks key transition.
source: Madon, 2021

claim: Main resources are reported from Groups J, I, K, E, D; I/J/K contribute about 60%, and D/E plus those contribute about 85%; deltaic sands dominate.
source: Madon, 2021

claim: Oils/condensates derive mainly from lower coastal plain fluvio-deltaic coal/coaly shale and lacustrine syn-rift shales; northwest is gas-prone, southeast more oil-prone.
source: Madon, 2021

claim: Remaining potential is not zero; paper estimates roughly 2 bboe yet to discover by 2020, but requires new play concepts.
source: Madon, 2021

claim: Malay Basin stratigraphy includes Groups A, B, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M (Group C absent — EPMI nomenclature). Group G is a marine-influenced transition unit between F and H. Group L is a regional seal for basin flank overpressure and the best lacustrine source rock.
source: Madon 2004, Madon 2010 GSM, Knova UM 2020, USGS OF99-50-T

claim: Group K is BOTH a fluvial reservoir (~16% of reserves) AND a lacustrine source rock (K-Source Facies, TOC 0.35-2.0 wt%, HI 137-403 with mixed Type II/III). Group L is best source (HI 300-400, lacustrine).
source: Madon 2010 GSM Bulletin — Organic facies variation in lacustrine source rocks

claim: Two overpressure compartments in Malay Basin: (1) Basin centre — top of OP at 1900-2000m in lower Group E, sealed by Group F shale, deeper compartment extends through Groups K, L, M; (2) Basin flank — top of OP at 2600-3000m, sealed by Group L shale.
source: Madon 2004 SPE 88455 — Overpressure History of Malay Basin

claim: Component 36 - Unknown-Space Mapping. Coverage is not uncertainty, coverage is not confidence. Coverage measures observational density, not statistical spread. Every pore pressure prediction MUST report coverage_score alongside confidence. Confidence=0.81 with coverage_score=0.0 = INVALID (HYPOTHESIS, not DERIVED).
source: F13 SOVEREIGN directive 2026-08-13 - Bekok Deep-1 coverage doctrine

claim: Bright spot = direct hydrocarbon indicator on 3D seismic = geophysical evidence of subsurface fluid. Presence = coverage EXISTS at that location. Absence of seismic = bright spot CANNOT exist (not not-detected). Platform wells need SEPARATE shallow gas assessment from exploration seismic.
source: F13 SOVEREIGN 2026-08-13 - bright spot as coverage witness

claim: Institutional narrative that attributes well incident to well-collision or formation-issue while omitting absence of pre-drill site survey or coverage gap = architectural lie. Any epistemic claim omitting what was NOT sampled is incomplete. F9 ANTIHANTU flag raised.
source: F13 SOVEREIGN 2026-08-13 - coverage-based lie detection

claim: Malay Basin CO2 risk: basin-wide produced-gas CO2 spans 0.92-5.5 mol%. CO2-dominated accumulations (40-90 mol%) occur only along basement-penetrating fault trends (Dulang-Melor, Bunga Raya-Bunga Pakma). Open area northern-ramp position avoids those trends -> CO2 risk assessed LOW-MODERATE, but by basin ANALOGUE judgement, not measurement.
source: Waples & Mahadir 1996 (GSM Bulletin 39) | North Malay Basin CO2 studies | GEOX MTJDA dossier

metadata.risk_rule: Any bounding fault that roots into basement = HIGH CO2 risk until tested.
metadata.falsifier: A basement-rooting bounding fault on a lead where CO2 remains below 6 mol%

claim: Malay Basin overpressure dual compartment: (1) basin centre top-OP at 1,900-2,000 m in lower Group E sealed by Group F shale, deeper compartment through Groups K/L/M; (2) basin flank top-OP at 2,600-3,000 m sealed by Group L shale. MTJDA sits on the northern ramp -> the FLANK model applies.
source: Madon 2004 SPE 88455 - Overpressure history of the Malay Basin | GEOX MTJDA dossier

metadata.operational_consequence: Pore-pressure prediction in the MTJDA open area must be built on the FLANK model. Importing basin-centre assumptions into depth conversion or mud-weight design is wrong by several hundred metres.
metadata.failure_family: Same class as the NW Sabah mobile-shale velocity trap (Vp 1.5-2.0 vs 2.8-3.5 km/s -> 200-500 m depth error).
metadata.note: Overlaps existing clm_overpressure_dual_compartment (claim store already held this). The ADDED content is the MTJDA-specific flank consequence, which was not previously registered.

claim: Deep syn-rift fairway in the MTJDA open area: Groups K/L/M sandstones sealed by Group L and M lacustrine shales, trapped in syn-rift fault blocks and stratigraphic pinchouts. Group K is dual reservoir AND source - which removes one risk element (charge) and adds another (seal must be effective intra-formationally, not regionally). Reservoir quality below ~3,000 m is compaction/deiagenesis degraded.
source: GEOX MTJDA dossier Fig.8 | Madon 1999 | USGS OF99-50-T

claim: MTJDA two trap families with different risk profiles: (a) fault-bounded anticlines from compressional inversion of syn-rift normal faults - hold the bulk of discovered resource, easy to image, but seal depends on fault seal capacity (shale gouge ratio) sensitive to clay-content estimates; (b) stratigraphic pinchouts where fluvial channels pass into flood-plain claystone - emerging, high stratigraphic risk, requires good seismic resolution and amplitude support.
source: Madon 1999 | GEOX MTJDA dossier regional narrative

claim: Malay Basin is a failed rift - extension began but never progressed to seafloor spreading. ~500 km x 200 km elongate Cenozoic basin, >14 km sediment in deepest centre, ~80,000 km2, ~40% of Malaysia's hydrocarbon resources, >700 exploration wells. MTJDA occupies the northern ramp margin, a shallower more gently structured position with thinner cover and different overpressure behaviour.
source: Madon 2021 (GSM Bulletin 72, doi:10.7186/bgsm72202106) | GEOX MTJDA dossier
